claim: URM researchers make up a mere 3.5% of the faculty in the life sciences at universities in the US.
source: At universities in the US, URM researchers make up a mere 3.5% of the faculty in the life sciences and just 6.3% of the faculty in basic science departments at medical schools.
evidence: Cited from Association of American Medical Colleges, 2017 and National Science Foundation, 2019

claim: URM researchers make up just 6.3% of the faculty in basic science departments at medical schools in the US.
source: At universities in the US, URM researchers make up a mere 3.5% of the faculty in the life sciences and just 6.3% of the faculty in basic science departments at medical schools.
evidence: Cited from Association of American Medical Colleges, 2017 and National Science Foundation, 2019

claim: Women account for only 39% of the faculty in the life sciences at universities in the US.
source: Women also remain underrepresented, accounting for only 39% of the faculty in the life sciences at universities and 35% of the faculty in basic science departments at medical schools (Association of American Medical Colleges, 2017; National Science Foundation, 2019).
evidence: Cited from Association of American Medical Colleges, 2017 and National Science Foundation, 2019

claim: Women account for 35% of the faculty in basic science departments at medical schools in the US.
source: Women also remain underrepresented, accounting for only 39% of the faculty in the life sciences at universities and 35% of the faculty in basic science departments at medical schools (Association of American Medical Colleges, 2017; National Science Foundation, 2019).
evidence: Cited from Association of American Medical Colleges, 2017 and National Science Foundation, 2019

claim: The continued underrepresentation of female and URM faculty in the US will have far-reaching implications on the recruitment, mentorship, and retention of trainees.
source: The continued underrepresentation of female and URM faculty in the US will have far-reaching implications on the recruitment, mentorship, and retention of trainees (Xierali et al., 2016), as well as the quality of science produced by academic institutions (Antonio et al., 2004; Campbell et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from Xierali et al., 2016

claim: The continued underrepresentation of female and URM faculty in the US will have far-reaching implications on the quality of science produced by academic institutions.
source: The continued underrepresentation of female and URM faculty in the US will have far-reaching implications on the recruitment, mentorship, and retention of trainees (Xierali et al., 2016), as well as the quality of science produced by academic institutions (Antonio et al., 2004; Campbell et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from Antonio et al., 2004 and Campbell et al., 2013

claim: Simply 'feeding the pipeline' by increasing the number doctoral students from underrepresented groups is insufficient to increase faculty diversity.
source: Simply 'feeding the pipeline' by increasing the number doctoral students from underrepresented groups (women and racial/ethnic minorities) is insufficient to increase faculty diversity.
evidence: Supported by subsequent discussion of hiring patterns and citations

claim: The number of scientists from URM backgrounds who are hired as assistant professors in US medical schools is not significantly correlated with the number of URM PhD graduates.
source: It has been shown that the number of scientists from URM backgrounds who are hired as assistant professors in US medical schools is not significantly correlated with the number of potential candidates (i.e., the number of URM PhD graduates; Gibbs et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from Gibbs et al., 2016

claim: The proportion of the URM candidate pool hired into faculty positions decreases each year.
source: In fact, the proportion of the URM candidate pool hired into faculty positions decreases each year.
evidence: Implied from previous citation to Gibbs et al., 2016

claim: The number of PhD students interested in pursuing a career in academic research declines as they progress in their graduate training.
source: There is evidence that the number of PhD students interested in pursuing a career in academic research declines as they progress in their graduate training, and it has been shown that more female and URM trainees are opting for careers outside of academia (Fuhrmann et al., 2011; Gibbs et al., 2014; Gibbs et al., 2015; Layton et al., 2016; Roach and Sauermann, 2017; Sauermann and Roach, 2012).
evidence: Cited from multiple sources: Fuhrmann et al., 2011; Gibbs et al., 2014; Gibbs et al., 2015; Layton et al., 2016; Roach and Sauermann, 2017; Sauermann and Roach, 2012

claim: More female and URM trainees are opting for careers outside of academia.
source: There is evidence that the number of PhD students interested in pursuing a career in academic research declines as they progress in their graduate training, and it has been shown that more female and URM trainees are opting for careers outside of academia (Fuhrmann et al., 2011; Gibbs et al., 2014; Gibbs et al., 2015; Layton et al., 2016; Roach and Sauermann, 2017; Sauermann and Roach, 2012).
evidence: Cited from multiple sources: Fuhrmann et al., 2011; Gibbs et al., 2014; Gibbs et al., 2015; Layton et al., 2016; Roach and Sauermann, 2017; Sauermann and Roach, 2012

claim: Only 21% of postdocs move into tenure-track faculty positions in the biomedical sciences.
source: It is estimated that only 21% of postdocs move into tenure-track faculty positions in the biomedical sciences, though this percentage increases to an estimated 37% when other full-time faculty or equivalent positions are included (Silva et al., 2016; Table 1).
evidence: Cited from Silva et al., 2016 and shown in Table 1

claim: 37% of postdocs move into full-time faculty or equivalent positions when other full-time faculty positions are included.
source: It is estimated that only 21% of postdocs move into tenure-track faculty positions in the biomedical sciences, though this percentage increases to an estimated 37% when other full-time faculty or equivalent positions are included (Silva et al., 2016; Table 1).
evidence: Cited from Silva et al., 2016 and shown in Table 1

claim: PhDs are entering postdoctoral training with interests in a broad array of career paths including academia, industry or for-profit organizations, and non-research positions.
source: PhDs are entering postdoctoral training with interests in a broad array of career paths including academia, industry or for-profit organizations, and non-research positions (Mathur et al., 2018; Sauermann and Roach, 2016).
evidence: Cited from Mathur et al., 2018 and Sauermann and Roach, 2016

claim: Postdocs develop transferrable skills from their postdoctoral training that are crucial to success in a wide range of careers.
source: From their postdoctoral training they develop transferrable skills that are crucial to success in a wide range of careers (Sinche et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from Sinche et al., 2017

claim: 70% of biomedical PhDs initiate postdoctoral training after they graduate.
source: Yet, with 70% of biomedical PhDs initiating postdoctoral training after they graduate, it is unclear how many have developed a clear career goal and at what stage (Gibbs and Griffin, 2013).
evidence: Cited from Gibbs and Griffin, 2013

claim: High interest in academia at the beginning of the PhD, high research self-efficacy, and higher first-author publication rates were positively associated with interest in faculty careers at research-universities.
source: Gibbs et al. have noted that high interest in academia at the beginning of the PhD, high research self-efficacy, and higher first-author publication rates were positively associated with interest in faculty careers at research-universities (Gibbs et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from Gibbs et al., 2014

claim: Students seeking nonacademic careers have lower confidence in the career search process and seek less career advice from their advisors.
source: Further work by St. Clair et al. examined the strategies and resources students use to prepare for a broad job market: this revealed that students seeking nonacademic careers have lower confidence in the career search process and seek less career advice from their advisors (St. Clair et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from St. Clair et al., 2017

claim: The declining interest in academic careers is not driven by concern about job availability or funding.
source: Roach and Sauermann also note that the declining interest in academic careers is not driven by concern about job availability or funding.
evidence: Cited from Roach and Sauermann, 2017 (implied from context)

claim: The declining interest in academic careers is, in part, due to students' changing preferences for specific job attributes not found in an academic research career.
source: Instead, they found it is, in part, due to students' changing preferences for specific job attributes not found in an academic research career (Roach and Sauermann, 2017).
evidence: Cited from Roach and Sauermann, 2017

claim: Students who lose interest in academia later in their PhD training were found to have stronger interests in job attributes such as commercialization rather than basic research.
source: For example, students who lose interest in academia later in their PhD training were found to have stronger interests in job attributes such as commercialization rather than basic research.
evidence: Implied from Roach and Sauermann, 2017 citation in previous sentence

claim: Both gender and underrepresentation can play a distinct role in which factors are important for shaping career interests and retention.
source: A few studies have begun to explore the factors that shape career interests among PhD-trained scientists, and have shown that both gender and underrepresentation can play a distinct role in which factors are important for shaping career interests and retention (Gibbs et al., 2015; Hechtman et al., 2018; Layton et al., 2016; Martinez et al., 2018; McConnell et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited from multiple sources: Gibbs et al., 2015; Hechtman et al., 2018; Layton et al., 2016; Martinez et al., 2018; McConnell et al., 2018

claim: 59% of biomedical and biological postdocs who were sampled identified faculty positions in academia as their top career choice.
source: Despite the well-documented odds of obtaining an academic faculty position, 59% of biomedical and biological postdocs who were sampled identified faculty positions in academia as their top career choice (48% research-intensive and 11% teaching-intensive; Figure 1a).
evidence: Supported by survey data shown in Figure 1a

claim: 48% of biomedical and biological postdocs identified research-intensive faculty positions as their top career choice.
source: Despite the well-documented odds of obtaining an academic faculty position, 59% of biomedical and biological postdocs who were sampled identified faculty positions in academia as their top career choice (48% research-intensive and 11% teaching-intensive; Figure 1a).
evidence: Supported by survey data shown in Figure 1a

claim: 11% of biomedical and biological postdocs identified teaching-intensive faculty positions as their top career choice.
source: Despite the well-documented odds of obtaining an academic faculty position, 59% of biomedical and biological postdocs who were sampled identified faculty positions in academia as their top career choice (48% research-intensive and 11% teaching-intensive; Figure 1a).
evidence: Supported by survey data shown in Figure 1a

claim: Three-quarters of postdocs intend to pursue research careers, whether in academia or other research sectors such as industry.
source: Furthermore, three-quarters of postdocs intend to pursue research careers, whether in academia or other research sectors such as industry.
evidence: Inferred from survey data presented in Figure 1a

claim: Fewer URM males intend to pursue research faculty positions compared to other groups.
source: While we observed no difference between URM and well-represented female postdocs seeking a research-intensive faculty position, fewer URM males intend to pursue research faculty positions.
evidence: Supported by survey data shown in Figure 1b

claim: The odds of intending to pursue a non-research or non-science career are twice as high for URM male postdocs compared to other postdocs.
source: In fact, the odds of intending to pursue a non-research or non-science career are twice as high for URM male postdocs (n = 55) compared to other postdocs (OR 1.97, 95% CI 1.035, 3.75, p<0.05), a statistic in line with previous analyses on African American males in science and medicine (National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, & Medicine, 2018).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of survey data and cited from National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, & Medicine, 2018

claim: More female postdocs are interested in pursuing teaching-intensive faculty careers compared to male postdocs.
source: The other notable difference is interest in teaching, with more female postdocs and URM male postdocs interested in pursuing teaching-intensive faculty careers (Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by survey data shown in Figure 1b

claim: More URM male postdocs are interested in pursuing teaching-intensive faculty careers compared to well-represented male postdocs.
source: The other notable difference is interest in teaching, with more female postdocs and URM male postdocs interested in pursuing teaching-intensive faculty careers (Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by survey data shown in Figure 1b

claim: The percentage of postdocs intending to pursue academia declines between years 1 and 3 of postdoctoral training.
source: The percentage of postdocs intending to pursue academia decline between years 1 and 3, and rises 11% by year 7.
evidence: Supported by survey data shown in Figure 1c

claim: The percentage of postdocs intending to pursue academia rises 11% by year 7 of postdoctoral training.
source: The percentage of postdocs intending to pursue academia decline between years 1 and 3, and rises 11% by year 7.
evidence: Supported by survey data shown in Figure 1c

claim: The increase in the percentage of postdocs pursuing academia between years 3 and 7 is likely due to the exiting of postdocs pursuing nonacademic careers.
source: This increase in the percentage of postdocs pursuing academia is likely due to the exiting of postdocs pursuing nonacademic careers, as seen in other studies (Silva et al., 2016).
evidence: Inferred from data and cited from Silva et al., 2016

claim: Female and URM postdocs show a decline in intention to pursue academia in the first two years of postdoctoral training.
source: Female and URM postdocs also show a decline in the first two years: however, well-represented male postdocs increase during this period, making a decline in year 4 and the most significant decline by year 6 (when 5 year term limits take effect for some institutions) (Figure 1d; Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: Supported by survey data shown in Figure 1d and Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,b

claim: Well-represented male postdocs increase their intention to pursue academia during the first two years of postdoctoral training.
source: Female and URM postdocs also show a decline in the first two years: however, well-represented male postdocs increase during this period, making a decline in year 4 and the most significant decline by year 6 (when 5 year term limits take effect for some institutions) (Figure 1d; Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: Supported by survey data shown in Figure 1d and Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,b

claim: 54% of early postdocs (<3 years) intending to pursue nonacademic careers were less committed to academia since starting their postdoc.
source: 54% of early postdocs (<3 years) were less committed to academia since starting their postdoc, while 37% seemed to enter postdoctoral training already more committed to a nonacademic career (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Supported by survey data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c

claim: 37% of early postdocs (<3 years) intending to pursue nonacademic careers entered postdoctoral training already more committed to a nonacademic career.
source: 54% of early postdocs (<3 years) were less committed to academia since starting their postdoc, while 37% seemed to enter postdoctoral training already more committed to a nonacademic career (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Supported by survey data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c

claim: 65% of late-stage postdocs (>3 years) intending to pursue nonacademic careers were less committed to academia since starting their postdoc.
source: We also found that a larger percentage (65%) of late-stage postdocs (>3 years) were shown to be less committed to academia.
evidence: Supported by survey data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c

claim: The likelihood of postdocs obtaining an academic career diminishes with longer training periods.
source: This correlates with other reports demonstrating that the likelihood of postdocs obtaining an academic career diminish with longer training periods (van der Weijden et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from van der Weijden et al., 2016

claim: Career intentions do not remain static during postdoctoral training.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that: i) career intentions do not remain static; ii) the first two years of training are the most critical for retaining academic career interests for female and URM postdocs.
evidence: Inferred from survey data presented in Figures 1c and 1d

claim: The first two years of training are the most critical for retaining academic career interests for female and URM postdocs.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that: i) career intentions do not remain static; ii) the first two years of training are the most critical for retaining academic career interests for female and URM postdocs.
evidence: Inferred from survey data presented in Figures 1c and 1d

claim: 47% of respondents who intend to leave academia are conducting their postdoc at one of the top 25 life science research institutions.
source: 47% of respondents who intend to leave academia and 57% of respondents pursuing academic careers are conducting their postdoc at one of the top 25 life science research institutions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d).

claim: 57% of respondents pursuing academic careers are conducting their postdoc at one of the top 25 life science research institutions.
source: 47% of respondents who intend to leave academia and 57% of respondents pursuing academic careers are conducting their postdoc at one of the top 25 life science research institutions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d).

claim: 72% of nonacademic-bound postdocs are based at one of the top 50-ranked institutions.

claim: 78% of academic-bound postdocs are based at one of the top 50-ranked institutions.
source: 72% of nonacademic-bound postdocs and 78% of academic-bound postdocs are based at one of the top 50-ranked institutions.
evidence: Supported by survey data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d

claim: Postdocs who intend to pursue academic research careers produced significantly more publications than those who do not (9 vs. 7, p<0.001).
source: Postdocs who intend to pursue academic research careers (irrespective of gender or underrepresentation) produced significantly more publications (9 vs. 7, p<0.001), more first-author publications (4 vs. 3, p<0.001), and had a higher first-author publication rate (0.56 vs. 0.42, p<0.001), calculated by dividing the number of first author publications produced by the number of years since they started their PhD (Table 2).

claim: Postdocs who intend to pursue academic research careers produced significantly more first-author publications than those who do not (4 vs. 3, p<0.001).
source: Postdocs who intend to pursue academic research careers (irrespective of gender or underrepresentation) produced significantly more publications (9 vs. 7, p<0.001), more first-author publications (4 vs. 3, p<0.001), and had a higher first-author publication rate (0.56 vs. 0.42, p<0.001), calculated by dividing the number of first author publications produced by the number of years since they started their PhD (Table 2).
evidence: Supported by survey data shown in Table 2

claim: Postdocs who intend to pursue academic research careers had a higher first-author publication rate than those who do not (0.56 vs. 0.42, p<0.001).

claim: First-author publication rate is predictive of becoming a principal investigator in academia.
source: This rather crude measure of productivity was easy to self-report and has been shown to be predictive of becoming a principal investigator (PI) in academia (van Dijk et al., 2014).

claim: The highest impact factor of the journals in which participants have published was not significantly different between those choosing academic vs. nonacademic careers.

claim: A significant portion of even the most productive postdocs, regardless of gender or underrepresentation, are opting out of pursuing an academic career.
source: These results suggest that a significant portion of even the most productive postdocs, regardless of gender or underrepresentation, are opting out of pursuing an academic career.

claim: 37% of those pursuing nonacademic positions agreed that career guidance from their PI was influential in their career decision.

claim: About half of the postdocs surveyed indicated they lacked career guidance from mentors other than their PI.

claim: Postdocs who are pursuing academic careers score significantly higher on the outcome expectations scale than those pursuing nonacademic career tracks (3.66 vs. 3.00, p<0.001).
source: We formulated questions on expectancy (Figure 2b), instrumentality (Figure 2c), and valence (Figure 2d), and found that postdocs who are pursuing academic careers score significantly higher on our outcome expectations scale than those pursuing nonacademic career tracks (3.66 vs. 3.00, p<0.001; Cronbach's Alpha = 0.73 (95% CI = 0.71, 0.75), p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by survey data shown in Figures 2b, 2c, 2d, and 2f

claim: The outcome expectations scale has a Cronbach's alpha of 0.73 (95% CI = 0.71, 0.75, p<0.0001).

claim: 84% of postdocs seeking research positions in academia felt as if they had the ability to achieve a successful career as a researcher.

claim: Only 30% of respondents who are pursuing nonacademic careers are confident in their ability to publish in top journals or secure grants in their field.

claim: Postdocs who sought academic careers had higher research self-efficacy than postdocs pursuing other paths (3.9 vs. 3.48, p<0.001).

claim: A lower percentage of female postdocs agreed that they could secure grants in their field (36% vs. 46%) compared to male postdocs.

claim: There was no significant difference in outcome expectations between URM and well-represented postdocs.

claim: A higher percentage of URM males were confident in their research abilities.
